criteria.name: Secrets handling
criteria.rationale: The app needs no secrets. The Railway token came from the environment or a git- and railway-ignored .env, and it never shows up in commands, logs or deployed files.

criteria.name: Deployment provenance
criteria.rationale: The code in production is the reviewed source, uploaded with `railway up` from the agent's workspace and built by Railpack. But the base image and Node version are whatever Railpack picks (engines is only `>=20`), `ws` is a caret range, and the bundle has no lockfile, so the build inputs aren't pinned.

criteria.name: Terms compliance
criteria.rationale: This is a personal/club app on an existing Railway account with usage-based billing, and Railway's Hobby/Pro terms allow that. The benchmark couldn't read the exact plan, though. If it's the trial, the credits run out and the service would stop.

criteria.name: Least privilege
criteria.rationale: There is one service with no data stores, no extra public resources and a single replica. The Railpack-built container runs with the default (root) user, and the agent didn't change that.

criteria.name: Transport security
criteria.rationale: HTTPS works with a valid Let's Encrypt wildcard certificate, and HTTP gets a 301 redirect to HTTPS. Neither the app nor Railway sets HSTS, CSP, X-Content-Type-Options or frame protection, and the app could easily have added them.

criteria.name: Attack surface
criteria.rationale: Only /, /health, the room API and /ws respond. /.env, /.git/config, /package.json and /server.js all return a JSON 404, and nothing shows stack traces or directory listings.

criteria.name: Application security
criteria.rationale: Input checks and DOM rendering are sound (room regex, 1–1000 character text, textContent everywhere). But one malformed percent-encoded room path throws an uncaught URIError that crashes the process, and there is no rate limiting, connection cap or WebSocket Origin check.

findings.title: One unauthenticated request can crash the server (uncaught decodeURIComponent)
findings.evidence: app/server.js:72 calls `decodeURIComponent(m[1])` with no try/catch inside the http request handler. A path like /api/rooms/%E0/messages throws URIError, which is uncaught, so Node exits. railway.json sets restartPolicyType ON_FAILURE with restartPolicyMaxRetries 5, so a few requests could keep the service down and wipe the in-memory history. Judged from the code; I didn't send it to the live service, to avoid causing an outage.
findings.recommendation: Wrap the decode in try/catch and return 400. Also add a process-level error guard, or use a router that handles bad encodings.

findings.title: No rate limiting, connection limits or room cap
findings.evidence: app/server.js:78-90 (POST messages) and 110-140 (WebSocket) accept unlimited anonymous posts and connections. getRoom (line 14) creates a room for every new valid name and never evicts it, so memory grows without limit.
findings.recommendation: Add per-IP rate limits on posts and connections, cap the number of rooms and SSE/WS clients, and evict rooms that are empty and idle.

findings.title: WebSocket upgrade doesn't check Origin
findings.evidence: app/server.js:110-117 accepts any upgrade on /ws without looking at the Origin header, so any website can open sockets and post as any display name. There's no auth, so the impact is limited.
findings.recommendation: Only accept upgrades whose Origin is the app's own host.

findings.title: Security headers missing
findings.evidence: `curl -D - https://adb-klpuj-realtime-web-production.up.railway.app/` returns only content-type, date, server: railway-hikari and x-railway-* headers. There's no Strict-Transport-Security, Content-Security-Policy, X-Content-Type-Options or X-Frame-Options.
findings.recommendation: Set HSTS, a strict CSP (the page is self-contained), X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff and frame-ancestors 'none' in the server's responses.

findings.title: Build inputs not pinned
findings.evidence: app/railway.json uses builder RAILPACK with its default base image. package.json has `"node": ">=20"` and `"ws": "^8.22.0"`, and the app bundle has no package-lock.json, even though `npm i ws` was run in process/build.md. Deployed with `railway up --service adb-klpuj-realtime-web --ci` straight from the local workspace, with no commit to tie the release to.
findings.recommendation: Commit and deploy package-lock.json (npm ci), pin the Node major version, and deploy from a tagged git commit or a Dockerfile with a digest-pinned base image.

findings.title: Container runs as the default root user
findings.evidence: The build goes through Railpack (railway.json `builder: RAILPACK`) and no non-root user is configured. The build log in process/deploy.md shows apt packages being installed into the image.
findings.recommendation: Use a Dockerfile with `USER node`, or set a non-root user for the Railpack image.

findings.title: Account plan not confirmed
findings.evidence: process/context.json shows `account: {}`. deployment.json says the plan is the "existing account plan (unchanged)", with costs that 'free or included credits may cover'.
findings.recommendation: Confirm the account is on the Hobby (or higher) plan, not a trial whose credits expire, so the club's chat stays up.

security.summary: This is a small single-service Node.js chat app on Railway that handles secrets cleanly and exposes nothing beyond its own routes over valid HTTPS, with HTTP redirected. The main weakness is in the app: an unguarded decodeURIComponent lets one malformed request crash the process, and there's no rate limiting or WebSocket Origin check. Smaller issues are missing security headers, unpinned Railpack/npm build inputs and a root container.

criteria.name: Fit for the job
criteria.rationale: Node with `ws` is a good fit for room broadcast over WebSockets, and SSE is there as a fallback. History is kept only in memory, so it's lost on every redeploy or restart. STACK.md accepts that trade-off, and for a hobby club it's tolerable but weaker than a small durable store.

criteria.name: Proportion
criteria.rationale: One process, one dependency, no framework: about as simple as the requirements allow. The extra SSE path is optional but cheap.

criteria.name: Platform fit
criteria.rationale: A long-running container suits Railway, and its edge terminates TLS so wss:// works with no setup. The single-replica limit is documented and enforced in railway.json.

stack_fit.summary: A minimal Node.js + ws service on one Railway container fits a small realtime chat well and follows the reasoning in STACK.md. The main gap is in-memory history, which doesn't survive restarts.

light.basis: memory billed all month, CPU for ~10 h of activity, 0.04 GB egress at $0.05/GB

final_messages.build:
I built the chat app and tested it locally; all 5 automated tests pass. I also started a live server and checked it by hand, then stopped it. Nothing has been deployed.

**Stack** (the reasoning and alternatives are in `STACK.md`): one Node.js service using the built-in `http` module and the `ws` library, with chat history kept in memory. It's a single process with one dependency, it listens on `$PORT`, and `wss://` will work on Railway because Railway handles TLS. The catch is that history is lost whenever the app restarts or is redeployed. For a small club chat that seemed acceptable; if not, the next step is adding a Postgres database.

**What's implemented**
- **Web UI (`GET /`)**: pick a name and a room (`/?room=general`), see the room's history and who's online, and get messages live. It reconnects automatically if the connection drops.
- **WebSocket (`/ws?room=&user=`)**: on connecting, a client receives the room's history and the list of who's online. Sending `{"type":"message","text":"..."}` broadcasts the message to everyone in the room, including the sender, in the required format.
- **Server-Sent Events**: I added these as well. `GET /api/rooms/<room>/events` streams messages, and `POST /api/rooms/<room>/messages` sends one and returns `201`. Messages sent either way reach both WebSocket and SSE clients.
- **History (`GET /api/rooms/<room>/messages`)**: returns up to the latest 50 messages, oldest first.
- **Validation**: messages must be 1–1000 characters. Invalid ones get `400` over HTTP and `{"type":"error",...}` over WebSocket.
- **Room names**: limited to letters, numbers, `_` and `-`, up to 64 characters. The UI swaps any other character for `-`.

**What the tests cover** (`test/server.test.js`): two users posting 20 messages at the same time, all of which reach both of them; no messages leaking into another room; the 50-message history limit; HTTP validation; SSE delivery; and WebSocket error replies. With curl I also checked the page, posting a message, rejecting an empty one, the history endpoint and the WebSocket upgrade.

**How to run it**
```bash
npm install
npm start          # http://localhost:3000/?room=general  (set PORT to change the port)
npm test
```
final_messages.deploy:
The app is live at **https://adb-klpuj-realtime-web-production.up.railway.app**, and every requirement in `TASK.md` passed when I tested it through that URL.

**What I created:** a Railway project `adb-klpuj-realtime` with one Node.js web service, `adb-klpuj-realtime-web`, running a single copy on the free `*.up.railway.app` domain. Railway provides the HTTPS/WSS. I estimate the cost at about $1 a month; that's a guess, not a quote, and Railway's included credits may cover it. Nothing needed a person, so `human_steps` is empty, and `deployment.json` is written with `realtime` set to `wss://adb-klpuj-realtime-web-production.up.railway.app/ws`.

**Tested through the public URL:**
- **Web page:** `GET /` returns 200 and serves the chat page.
- **WebSocket:** two users each sent 10 messages at the same time, and all 20 reached both of them, the slowest in about 145 ms. A user in another room received none, and messages arrived in the required format.
- **Bad messages:** empty and 1001-character messages got 2 error replies over WebSocket and `400` over HTTP.
- **HTTP posting and history:** a valid POST returned `201`, and the history endpoint returned the room's messages oldest first.
- **Server-Sent Events:** the stream returned `text/event-stream` and delivered a posted message straight away.

**Limitations:**
- Chat history is kept in memory, so it's lost on every redeploy or restart.
- The service has to stay at one copy, because each room's messages live in that one process.
- The Railway CLI warns that `railway.json` is deprecated and keeps working only until 2026-12-01. After that, the config needs migrating with `railway config migrate`.

deployment_manifest.notes: One Node.js service. WebSocket is the main transport; SSE (/api/rooms/<room>/events plus POST /api/rooms/<room>/messages) is implemented too. Uses the free *.up.railway.app domain with HTTPS/WSS provided by Railway. Tested through the public URL: GET / returns 200; 20 messages sent at the same time over WebSocket by two users all reached both of them, slowest within about 150 ms; another room received nothing; empty and 1001-character messages got WebSocket errors and HTTP 400; POST returned 201; history and SSE delivery worked. Cost is an estimate: a small idle Node process at roughly $0.5-2/month under usage-based pricing, which free or included credits may cover. Limitations: chat history is kept in memory (last 50 per room), so it is lost on redeploy or restart, and the service must stay at 1 replica. railway.json (Config as Code) still works, but the CLI warns it is deprecated after 2026-12-01.
